stories.headline: A first-time World Series champion? What Brewers-Rays means
stories.summary: At the final out of this Fall Classic, the Brewers or Rays will be celebrating their first title. We dive into the historic significance.
stories.body:
This World Series matchup between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays feels inevitable.

On the other hand, it feels impossible.

The Brewers were MLB's best team in the regular season, rolling to a franchise-record 103 wins and posting the top run differential in the sport. They're young, athletic and possess a quintessential modern bullpen full of hard-throwing relievers. They have appeared in eight of the past nine postseasons, had the best record in the majors last year and got better in 2026 as Jacob Misiorowski matured into the likely National League Cy Young winner. It should not be a surprise they're here.

The Rays, meanwhile, have been one of baseball's most successful franchises since their initial breakout season in 2008. They won 98 games this season, the most in the American League, and though they missed the playoffs in 2024 and 2025, they had made them five years in a row prior to that. They're young, athletic and possess one of MLB's best closers in Bryan Baker and one of the top power hitters in Junior Caminero. While not many picked the Rays to reach the World Series before the season, it should not be a surprise they're here.

And yet ... the Brewers ranked 19th in payroll and play in the sport's smallest metro market. The Rays are 28th in payroll. That feels unbelievable in a world where owners -- with a labor fight and lockout looming in the offseason -- are arguing the sport isn't fair. The historic significance of this World Series goes beyond the size of each team's payroll though. Neither franchise has won a World Series, so the list of teams without a title will drop from five to four when this year's champion is crowned. The Brewers, in their 57th season in Milwaukee, will be looking to end one of the longest title droughts in the sport, while the Rays are hoping their third World Series trip is the charm. We get the best teams in each league facing off, a rarity in the expanded playoffs of the wild-card era.

It has a chance to be a classic World Series.

No. 1 vs. No. 1

Let's start here. For purists who appreciate the grind and importance of the 162-game season, this is a throwback-style World Series: The teams that won the most games in each league will be playing each other. Imagine that. In the wild-card era, which began in 1995, this has happened just six times now in 32 years:

1995: Braves over Cleveland
1999: Yankees over Braves
2013: Red Sox over Cardinals
2020: Dodgers over Rays
2024: Dodgers over Yankees
2026: Brewers vs. Rays

The Brewers and Rays deserve to be here; they aren't just two teams that got hot at the right time like we've seen some Octobers. If rewarding the grind of the regular season is your jig, you should be dancing about this matchup.

Beyond that, these are two really good teams. Here are the top combined World Series matchups since 1995 based on combined winning percentage:

1. 2020: Dodgers (43-17, .717) over Rays (40-20, .667)

2. 1995: Braves (90-54, .625) over Cleveland (100-44, .694)

3. 1998: Yankees (114-48, .704) over Padres (98-64, .605)

4. 2017: Astros (101-61, .623) over Dodgers (104-58, .642)

5. 2004: Red Sox (98-64, .605) over Cardinals (105-57, .648)

6. 2026: Brewers (103-59, .636) vs. Rays (98-64, .605)

6. 1999: Yankees (98-64, .605) over Braves (103-59, .636)

Sure, there is no household name such as Shohei Ohtani to draw in casual fans, but for die-hards it's a fun showdown between teams that play an exciting and attractive brand of baseball and it could pick up more interest as momentum builds throughout like the Blue Jays-Dodgers matchup did last season.

The expanded playoffs don't always lead to the most enticing World Series, so fans should savor this matchup. Just since the playoffs were expanded to 12 teams in 2022, the No. 6 seed has reached the World Series (the 2022 Phillies) and there was an all-wild-card series in 2023 between the 90-win Rangers and 84-win Diamondbacks.

World Series history can essentially be broken into four eras that have greatly affected the odds of the top team in each league advancing to the World Series:

The pennant era, 1903-1968

Format: The league winner advanced directly to the World Series.

Average World Series matchup: 1.0 (AL) vs. 1.0 (NL)

Percentage of No. 1 vs. No. 1: 100%

Obviously, in this era, the team with the best record won the pennant and advanced directly to the World Series.

The LCS era, 1969-1993

Format: Four playoff teams, two division winners in each league.

Average World Series matchup: 1.7 (AL) vs. 1.7 (NL)

Percentage of No. 1 vs. No. 1: 36% (9 out of 25)

This is considered by some as the golden era of postseason play, although since divisions weren't always equal, there could still be a surprise team in the World Series. The 1973 Mets made it after finishing 82-79, and the 1987 Twins had just the fifth-best record in the AL at 85-77 but won their division -- and then the World Series.

Wild-card era, 1995-2011

Format: Four playoff teams in each league (three division winners, one wild card).

Average World Series matchup: 2.2 (AL) vs. 2.6 (NL)

Percentage of No. 1 vs. No. 1: 12% (2 of 17)

The odds of the top teams meeting went down -- with nearly half the World Series in this era (eight of 17) not featuring one of the top teams from either league. The NL went seven straight years, from 2005 to 2011, without a top seed reaching the World Series, reaching the nadir in 2006 when the 83-79 Cardinals, owner of the fifth-best record in the league, reached the World Series -- and won it.

Expanded wild-card era, 2012-2026

Format: Five playoff teams through 2021 (eight in 2020), six since 2022

Average World Series matchup: 1.9 (AL) vs. 2.9 (NL)

Percentage of No. 1 vs. No. 1: 27% (4 of 15)

For whatever reason, there have been more No. 1-vs.-No. 1 matchups in this era, even as the playoffs expanded. This era did feature the first all-wild-card World Series between the Giants and Royals in 2014 -- neither team won 90 games -- but including the Brewers this October, seven 100-win teams have reached the World Series since 2016 (and the 2020 Dodgers on Rays played at a 100-win pace in the pandemic-shortened season).

You could argue that this era has presented the best of both worlds of playoff baseball: the random nature of a postseason tournament, but not so random that great teams never reach the World Series.

The longest droughts

The Brewers are in their 57th season in Milwaukee. The Rays are in their 29th season in Tampa Bay. Neither franchise has won a World Series. The last time we had this kind of World Series matchup was in 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals.

But while you'll surely hear that fact mentioned throughout the World Series, it depends on how you look at such things. Franchises relocate and cities sometimes get new teams. Milwaukee -- the city -- won a World Series in 1957 when the Braves were champions. Does that count? The New York Giants last won a World Series in 1954, but the San Francisco Giants, who relocated in 1958, didn't win until 2010. Did San Francisco fans care about 1954 while waiting for the first championship parade in their city?

If we use that city-based history, the last five World Series before this year between cities that had never won:

2010: San Francisco Giants (51) over Texas Rangers (37)

2002: Anaheim Angels (40) over San Francisco Giants (47)

(We'll treat Anaheim as separate from L.A. for this exercise.)

1992: Toronto Blue Jays (15) over Atlanta Braves (26)

1980: Philadelphia Phillies (76) over Kansas City Royals (11)

1920: Cleveland (16) over Brooklyn Robins (16)

The number in parentheses is the number of seasons each team had played in that city prior to the World Series year in question. (For the original 16 franchises, we start with the first World Series in 1903.) The Rangers, for example, started out as the Washington Senators in 1961, but moved to Texas in 1972, so their clock starts in 1972.

So, for 2026, we get the Brewers at 56 seasons played without a title and the Rays at 28 -- that adds up to 84 seasons without a title, close to but not quite matching the 88 seasons between the Giants and Rangers in 2010 or the 87 between the Angels/Giants and Phillies/Royals.

If we consider franchise droughts -- regardless of relocations -- since a last World Series title, this year's matchup comes as the seventh-longest combined drought World Series:

1. 2016 (174 seasons): Cubs (107) vs. Indians (67)

2. 2005 (130): White Sox (88) vs. Astros (42)

3. 2004 (106): Red Sox (85) vs. Cardinals (21)

4. 2010 (104): Giants (56) vs. Rangers (48)

5. 1975 (90): Red Sox (56) vs. Reds (34)

6. 1980 (87): Phillies (76) vs. Royals (11)

7. 2026 (85): Brewers (57) vs. Rays (28)

The strange case of the Milwaukee Brewers

Why 57 seasons instead of 56 for the Brewers? Because the franchise began in 1969 as the Seattle Pilots. How the franchise landed in Milwaukee in the first place is one of the wildest stories in MLB history. In a roundabout way, Brewers fans can thank Charlie Finley, the controversial and eclectic owner of the A's.

When Finley moved the A's from Kansas City to Oakland after the 1967 season, Missouri Senator Stuart Symington threatened MLB's antitrust exemption unless a replacement team was given to Kansas City. The American League quickly granted an expansion franchise to Kansas City for the 1969 season but needed a second team.

Seattle was awarded the second AL franchise, but the ownership consortium was underfunded and soon running out of money. A new domed stadium had been approved by local voters but got delayed, so the Pilots had to play in Sick's Stadium, a rundown minor league park in need of an overhaul. On Opening Day, workers could still be heard pounding nails into wooden bleachers in the outfield. If attendance got too high -- rarely a problem -- the water pressure stopped working.

At the World Series, a deal was reached to sell the team to a Bud Selig-led group of Milwaukee businessmen who had initially been hopeful of landing one of the National League expansion franchises in 1969 (which instead went to San Diego and Montreal). Fearful of another lawsuit, the American League tried to find new local owners in Seattle. The Pilots went to spring training in 1970 in Arizona. The franchise was also in bankruptcy court, unable to pay its debts. If players weren't paid, they would become free agents.

As the story goes, the team's equipment truck left Arizona and stopped in Utah, awaiting the word on whether to turn left for Seattle or right for Milwaukee. With the regular season days away, the court ruled that the Pilots were bankrupt. The sale for $10.8 million to the Selig group was now the only viable solution and the team headed to Milwaukee. "Ten eight!" Selig told author Dan Okrent. "For Steve Hovley and Jerry McNertney!"

After a string of losing seasons upon moving to Milwaukee, the Brewers reached their only World Series in 1982 -- the team known as Harvey's Wallbangers, after manager Harvey Kuenn. Led by MVP Robin Yount, Paul Molitor, Gorman Thomas and Cecil Cooper, they had scored the most runs in the majors since 1953 and the city held a parade for their runner-up finish.

One remnant of the Pilots remains to this day: the team's original blue-and-yellow colors.

stories.headline: Man United players get Thursday day off despite Como thrashing - sources
stories.summary: Manchester United's first-team squad will report back for training on Friday after being given a day off today following the humiliating 4-1 Champions League defeat against Como, sources have told ESPN.
stories.body:
Manchester United's first-team squad will report back for training on Friday after being given a day off today following the humiliating 4-1 Champions League defeat against Como, sources have told ESPN.

The result against the Serie A side was United's heaviest Champions League loss since a 4-0 reverse against Barcelona in November 1994 and leaves Michael Carrick's team in 21st position in the League Phase table after one win and two defeats in their opening three games in the competition.

But despite the magnitude of the defeat against Cesc Fàbregas' side, which led to captain Bruno Fernandes criticising the team's tactics -- Carrick responded by questioning the "running" of his players -- sources have said that the players will take their pre-arranged day off today before preparing for Sunday's Premier League home clash with Bournemouth on Friday.

United's flight back from Italy landed at Manchester at 12.20 a.m. on Thursday morning and sources have said that the decision to give the players a day off was based on recovery ahead of the weekend fixture against Bournemouth, who are in Europa League action against AC Milan on Thursday.

United are winless in their last seven games in all competitions and have lost four of those fixtures, against Manchester City, Brighton, Atlético Madrid and Como.

They go into the Bournemouth game sitting 13th in the Premier League having won just one league game all season with fitness concerns over several players including Luke Shaw, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, Lisandro Martínez, Ayden Heaven and Benjamin Sesko.

- Tielemans: 'Everything missing' in Utd's Como loss

- Champions League talking points: What to make of the Man Utd mess

- Carragher slams Fernandes for Carrick criticism

"I'm frustrated, more than frustrated. I'm really angry, to be honest," Carrick said after Thursday's game.

"But you've got to move on, you've got to deal with what's next and see what that looks like.

"At this moment in time, there's a lot to do before that next game, to get the team ready, because that was a difficult night for everyone."

stories.headline: Wysh List: Why NHL fighting is up -- and getting noticed
stories.summary: Through 120 games, there were 34 games with one or more fights, up over the last two seasons (25 and 26).
stories.body:
The boys are fighting.

According to the NHL, there has been an uptick in on-ice fisticuffs this season. Through 120 games, there were 34 games with one or more fights. That's up over last season (25) and the 2024-25 season (26).

"Definitely way more fights," one NHL veteran player told ESPN. "Way more physicality and competitiveness. Which I think is great for the league, because it's something that sets the NHL apart from all the other major sports leagues."

This is true. I'm not sure how many people tuned into NBA opening night to see if LeBron was going to throw hands with Karl-Anthony Towns to make an impression on his new teammates in Philly. The NHL's biggest stars will, however, punch people in the face.

Nathan MacKinnon of the Colorado Avalanche led the NHL with 53 goals last season and was second in ESPN's top 100 player ranking for this season. Last Tuesday, he sat in the Colorado dressing room with stitches across his bloody nose and a throbbing bruise under his left eye after a fight with Dallas Stars center Roope Hintz.

"That was crazy," said Matt Rempe of the New York Rangers, a noted pugilist that was in awe of MacKinnon-Hintz I. "They were both just chucking there, they were both just throwing bombs. Two skilled guys who were throwing, so it was pretty awesome."

It was MacKinnon's second fight of the season, having previously traded blows with Los Angeles Kings defenseman Brandt Clarke.

"The way we all grow up in the Maritimes is pretty gritty, Most guys from that area are feisty. I think it's good to do it sometimes. I might be done for the year, but I guess you never know," MacKinnon said after his second bout. "Getting punched is not that fun. But the guys seemed to like it, so maybe I'll do it a couple more times."

ESPN analyst Erik Johnson played with MacKinnon for 11 seasons and won the Stanley Cup with him in 2022.

"I'm actually surprised he doesn't fight more. He's so intense and he'd be the first to admit he has a screw loose. When that screw wiggles loose, you don't want to be in his path," Johnson said.

As Johnson noted, MacKinnon added Muay Thai to his training regimen, which may be a factor in his recent pugilism. He also thinks Nate's two fights might have created a copycat effect in the NHL this season.

"When you see a guy like MacKinnon do it, maybe that has a trickle-down effect to other players being like, 'Oh, I can do this too,'" he said.

There are a lot of theories why fighting might be on the rise in the NHL this season. One veteran player said that it's a surefire way to instantly create chemistry with teammates.

"Whether you're on a new team and you're trying to establish yourself with that team, who want to show that you're all-in," he said. "You want to have your teammates appreciate you and standing up for your buddy or for the big hits. I think that's part of it, the camaraderie."

Another player told ESPN that fights help snap some players into a more competitive mindset.

"I know there's a few guys around the league that want to make sure they get a fight in early in the season, just to remind them of the physicality. Sort of an, 'I can still do this,'" the player said. "Nobody wants to fight in preseason, because it's pointless. But in your first early regular-season games, if something happens and there's an opportunity, there's a fight."

About that preseason: Daniel Gallant, who runs HockeyFights.com, believes the league's truncated training camps -- thanks to a move to an 84-game season -- could be an influence.

"I think that opened the door for some players to want to make an impact and impression," he said.

According to HockeyFights, last season said the most unique players register a fight (288) since the 2013-14 campaign. Gallant's theory is that teams are finding talent to fill their lineup that can skate well and set the tone physically.

"To me, fighting in hockey sits at a bit of a tipping point," he said. "With the aforementioned increase in players willing to drop the gloves, the chance for more exciting fights coming on any given night increases."

Of course, the most frequent fighters don't have the ice time or accolades of a Nathan MacKinnon. Players like Columbus Blue Jackets forward Mathieu Olivier and Boston Bruins forward Mark Kastelic (tied for the league lead with 10 fights last season) drop the gloves with frequency. Gallant cites Arber Xhekaj (Montreal Canadiens), Scott Sabourin (Tampa Bay Lightning) and Jack McBain (Utah Mammoth) as fighters worth watching.

McBain already had a fight of the year candidate with Edmonton Oilers forward Trent Frederic, with both players absolutely unloading haymakers before leaving for their dressing rooms. Oilers star Connor McDavid could be seen smiling widely as he tapped his stick on the boards in appreciation.

It's worth asking: Is hockey fighting having a moment after years of decline?

Maybe for fans outside of the hockey bubble.

Consider that McBain vs. Frederic was the No. 2 TikTok video across all ESPN accounts last week. Not just hockey -- everything, with the NFL, college football and the MLB playoffs in full swing.

The greatest evidence of this uptick in popularity was back in 2025, when three fights in nine seconds between the USA and Canada launched the 4 Nations Face-Off into becoming a massive success ... while launching the Tkachuk brothers into a successful podcasting side-hustle. Of course, it helps that the Tkachuks are both stars and among the best offensive players in the NHL.

It's an interesting dynamic when goal-scorers fight. The 2004 Stanley Cup Final is known for two things: Existing on the precipice of the lockout, and having been the series where Calgary's Jarome Iginla and Tampa Bay's Vincent Lecavalier had an unexpected and epic throwdown.

I remember talking to San Jose Sharks players about watching Joe Thornton fight, as he averaged one or two annually for his first dozen seasons. They'd get up on the bench and understand that Jumbo has set the tone.

"I think it surprises you when you see guys that you wouldn't expect to fight end up fighting. That would definitely get you fired up," Johnson said. "Don't get me wrong: You're equally pumped when you have a guy on your team known for fighting that does his job. But I think it gives you a little boost seeing one of your best players do it, for sure."

MacKinnon is the unquestioned tone-setter in Colorado. Watching him fight -- twice! -- was as much for the Avalanche as it was for his own catharsis.

I asked one NHL player, who has never been MacKinnon's teammate, about his fights.

"If I'm on Colorado, I'm like, 'Wow, this guy is setting the tone,'" the player said. "He lost in the Olympics last year. [The Avs] lost in the playoffs. It looks like he's a man on a mission and willing to do whatever it takes. It's not like he's just doing it for dumb reasons."

Gallant likes a good superstar hockey fight. "It reminds you of the pure emotion some of these games carry. A guy like Tage Thompson of the Buffalo Sabres has had eight spirited bouts and he doesn't hold back. I imagine he'll have a few more as the years roll on," he said.

As far as stars that haven't fought yet, Gallant would like see what Oilers center Leon Draisaitl can do. His teammate, McDavid, hasn't had an NHL fight -- his last recorded bout on HockeyFights happened in 2014 while with the OHL Erie Otters. Macklin Celebrini, the consensus choice for the next face of the NHL, doesn't have an entry on his HockeyFights page while playing in his third NHL season. When he has his first fight, that clip probably goes supernova, given Mack's popularity.

OK, let's make that if he has his first fight. Or ever fights at all.

Teams by and large don't want their star players throwing punches. That goes for MacKinnon, too. "I think as the season goes on, you would see him do it less and less, just because it's very important to be healthy going into the playoffs," Johnson said.

Hockey fights are dangerous. Their infrequency in 2026 in comparison to previous decades should be lauded from a player safety perspective. As late as 2008-09, over 41% of all games featured a fight. That total was just 19% last season. I've written about factors in that decline before, with rules changes and the construction of team rosters as the main drivers.

While there's been a slight uptick in recent years, fighting remains infrequent in relation to how things used to be. I'd argue it's that infrequency that makes bouts like McBain vs. Frederic break through to general sports fans, or puts the spotlight on a player like MacKinnon when he fights. The NHL has gotten to a point where fighting remains part of the game but doesn't define the game, like back in the 1970s when the sport was a caricature of itself.

Many of the people I spoke with about this increase in fighting to start the season expect the trend to ebb by the end of the season. According to HockeyFights, the average number of fights per game has ranged between 0.23 and 0.25 for the last five seasons.

"I also just think it's cyclical, too. Some years are going to be up more than others," Johnson said. "But it is interesting to see that it's up this year."

WINNERS AND LOSERS
WINNER: Revenge Games
Brady Tkachuk's return to Ottawa may not have been the most bilious homecoming in recent NHL history -- John Tavares' first game at Nassau Coliseum as a Maple Leafs holds that title belt, what with the rubber snakes tossed at him -- but it came close for sheer nastiness. The Ottawa fans chanted "eff" Brady and his podcast, as well as about him eating crayons; they brought signs mocking his fealty to brother Matthew and his playoff choke job; and, in the greatest tradition of these spiteful nights, they placed totems of Brady in arena urinals, from hockey cards to jersey nameplates.

Brady Tkachuk made the night even more special by leaning into the villainy. He scored Florida's lone goal to give them a 1-0 lead and temporarily mute the crowd. He had a Grinch-like grin when boos rained down during stoppages. By proclaiming in his podcast that he intended to donate any jerseys thrown on the ice to a local charity, he incepted Senators fans to throw several of them. What a night. Hockey!

LOSER: Jumbotron Tributes
What happened to our Revenge Game oasis? When Mitch Marner made his acrimonious return to Toronto as a Golden Knight, the fans parked their booing and chants during his Jumbotron tribute video, even cheering Marner before getting back to the spite soon afterwards.

But on Brady Tkachuk Night, the fans in Ottawa jeered through the entirety of the Senators' video tribute to their former captain, leading to surreal images like Brady Tkachuk in a surgical mask visiting local children while the soundtrack is overwhelmed by hateful jeering. Again, hockey!

WINNER: Good lookin' Manny Malhotra
The fantasy sports site Rotogrinders did one of our favorite things recently: Creating an arbitrary sports ranking using a convoluted methodology. In this case, they ranked the most handsome NHL head coaches using a recipe of "Google's MediaPipe Face Mesh" and "468 facial reference points" and "four neoclassical and two landmark-based," which does sound better than "we threw a dart."

Based on this intricate system, Vancouver Canucks coach Manny Malhotra was ranked as the league's most handsome coach, followed closely by Vegas Golden Knights bench boss Ryan Craig. It's here we'll note that they're both in their first seasons as NHL head coaches, which explains a lot.

LOSER: Rick Bowness
The problem with putting your team on blast only a handful of games into the season is that a coach runs the risk of (a) not being able to effectively do it again and (b) potentially losing the team rather than lighting a fire under them.

Bowness has called out the Columbus Blue Jackets in public and in private, and the season is still spiraling. A mutual parting of ways seems like an inevitability if the Blue Jackets serve up a few more stinkers like that effort against Toronto this week.

WINNER: Vancouver Goldeneyes

In last week's column, we confessed our displeasure with the new PWHL Vegas jerseys. So it's only fair that we acknowledge the absolute perfection of these Vancouver Goldeneyes sweaters, built around a top tier hockey logo. A jersey worthy of the greatness that is KK Harvey.

LOSER: Cryptic marketing

We're very much looking forward to the Fanatics Hometown Remix jerseys that are coming soon. They were teased this week, as 31 teams released images of their new sweaters along with cryptic messages that needed to be descrambled -- like this Maple Leafs one that reads "It's Always About The Leafs."

I don't know ... I guess it works in theory. But it has very strong "Be Sure To Drink Your Ovaltine" energy.

FAVORITE ON-ICE MOMENT
Watching Connor McDavid, Leon Draisaitl, Zach Hyman and Evan Bouchard operate in a 4-on-3 power play in overtime is like having someone crank a Jack-in-the-Box that also plays your favorite song. Like, it's just a matter of time before it pops, as Bouchard did with the game-winner against Minnesota. It's poetry.

It was also a reminder of a plank in my platform: That we scrap the overtime and shootout for dueling power plays, which is closer to what we watched in the previous 60 minutes. But that's a column for another time.

FAVORITE OFF-ICE MOMENT
We're officially giving Calgary Flames netminder Devin Cooley the "Ilya Bryzgalov Award For Goalie Who Should Absolutely Keep Talking."

After blessing the hockey world with "nothing matters, nobody cares, we're all going to die" as a calming mantra last season, Cooley went viral again for this interview in which he "felt nothing" in a recent game because his "conscious brain" is bad at playing goal in comparison to his "unconscious brain," which is apparently Vezina-worthy. He expanded on this on a Q&A with Sportsnet.

Anaheim Ducks at Philadelphia Flyers

Saturday, Oct. 24, 1 p.m. ET (NHL Network)

Almost-Flyer Leo Carlsson plays in Philadelphia for the first time since the Flyers made him the highest paid player in the NHL this season thanks to their offer sheet. On the undercard: The always interesting matchup between Flyers star Trevor Zegras and his former team. He scored two goals against Anaheim at home last season.

Sunday, Oct. 25, 10 p.m. ET (ESPN+)

Now that we've seen how Ottawa fans have greeted the return of a former captain who was traded to play with his brother after informing his team he wasn't going to sign a new contract with them, Quinn Hughes plays in Vancouver for the first time following those exact circumstances. Well, save for the whole "playing with his brothers" thing. That comes later.

Boston Bruins at Carolina Hurricanes

Tuesday, Oct. 27, 7 p.m. ET (ESPN)

The Bruins were 7-2-1 in their first 10 games of the season, with the seventh best offense and fourth best defense in the NHL during that span. The defending Stanley Cup champions will be a good measuring stick for coach Marco Sturm's Bruins, in their first meeting of the season.

PUCK HEADLINES
Dateline: Winnipeg
Let's talk Connor Hellebuyck.

The Winnipeg Jets goaltender's suspension ends this Friday. That's not an arbitrary end date. According to sources, Hellebuyck informed the Jets on Oct. 2 that he intended to end his training camp holdout and return to the team. They promptly used a cause in the CBA that gives teams power to suspend players who have "not received permission to be absent from training camp," with the suspension being at "a reasonable length."

I had one NHL agent wonder if Hellebuyck and his representation were aware of this CBA clause, given that he's lost upwards of $900,000 and gained nothing insofar as leverage. At least Dylan Larkin had other fan bases desirously chanting his name.

Not a single source to whom I spoke this week believed that Hellebuyck would be traded before Friday, and that he'll end up collecting his paycheck while remaining back in Michigan, where ESPN's Emily Kaplan said he's been training.

It's been interesting to hear Winnipeg players creak the door open for a possible return to the team. Seeking reconciliation with estranged acquaintances is a basic human response -- some might say a character flaw -- and completely understandable when a player who has been in Winnipeg for 12 seasons decides to peace out.

Kyle Connor, a U.S. national teammate with Hellebuyck, has generally seemed devastated by the betrayal -- Hellebuyck was in his wedding party. Captain Adam Lowry has been more diplomatic, while acknowledging the extremely difficult healing that would have to happen should Hellebuyck return.

(Speaking of nuptials: Hellebuyck attended Lowry's wedding in July with a number of current teammates, with his desire to leave Winnipeg already widely reported by that point. I've sort of been obsessed with this. Did the Lowrys keep Hellebuyck at the same table seating for the reception or does a trade request put him in the back with the weird cousins instead of, like, next to Cole Perfetti?)

I've heard two opposing views on why a Hellebuyck deal hasn't happened yet. The first is that it's the player's fault: That Hellebuyck, who has a no-movement clause, wants to play for a Stanley Cup contender. Like, a sure thing team in the Carolina or Vegas or Florida sense. There are teams that have had talks with the Jets like Utah, Buffalo and Los Angeles, but they're not the level of contender Hellebuyck seeks. Again, that's from a few sources.

Other sources have indicated that it's GM Kevin Cheveldayoff holding up things here, as Hellebuyck would accept a move to places like Buffalo or Los Angeles. But Cheveldayoff wants to hit a grand slam with his most tradable asset, and he's yet to be offered a deal that rises to that standard from a team for whom Hellebuyck is willing to play.

I tend to believe the latter scenario is the catalyst for this stalemate. I've heard the ask from the Jets is astronomical, and frankly that's justified given Hellebuyck's accomplishments. One last note: The NHLPA told me it wanted to see how it played out after his suspension ends before commenting on the Hellebuyck situation. I'd be surprised if there's a grievance filed in the near term, what with Hellebuyck getting paid not to play. There's precedent for that. But the question is how long that'll last.

Dateline: Detroit
As I reported this week, disgruntled former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin has now expanded his list of potential destinations to at least 10 teams.

We knew about the first three that he gave Detroit in the offseason: The Florida Panthers, Minnesota Wild and Vegas Golden Knights. The list is now expanded to the Carolina Hurricanes, Colorado Avalanche, Dallas Stars, New Jersey Devils, Tampa Bay Lightning, Utah Mammoth and Washington Capitals. Again, these are teams to whom Larkin would accept a trade. We don't know how deep talks have gone with any of them.

Toronto-based writer Jeff Veillette noted that Larkin's list includes nine of the top 10 teams in current Stanley Cup betting odds, with only the Edmonton Oilers excluded -- sources have told ESPN that Larkin doesn't want a trade to a Canadian team, despite the desires of Montreal fans.

One team I'm fascinated by on his list are the Capitals. They're off to a somewhat middling start. GM Chris Patrick has been very aggressive in adding talent to his lineup, from Pierre-Luc Dubois and Jacob Chychrun to Jordan Kyrou and Boone Jenner. He has a robust pipeline of young talent that could entice the Red Wings, plus an NHL center that can help them now in Dylan Strome, who is signed through next season ($5 million AAV) and has no trade protection.

Ultimately, I think the Capitals would rather upgrade their back end in their quest for a second Stanley Cup. But as always, they're one to keep an eye on.

Formula 1 heads to Texas for the United States Grand Prix, with the championship battle set to heat up at the Circuit of the Americas.

Max Verstappen claimed his second victory this season after winning the Singapore Grand Prix for the first time.

Kimi Antonelli continued to extend his lead in the title championship to 102 points from Mercedes teammate George Russell, and there is a mathematical chance he will be able to clinch the title in Austin.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 18th round.

How to watch

Every practice and qualifying session as well as the race itself will be available to watch on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the United States Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Circuit of the Americas

The Circuit of the Americas first hosted the United States Grand Prix in 2012, to mark the end of a five year wait since the race at Indianapolis.

Mario Andretti, who won the world championship in 1978, opened the track and it has become a popular race among drivers and fans alike with plenty of overtaking action and drama.

COTA is a varied circuit with straights, esses through to sector two, and a series of hair-pins in sector three. The high-speed corners takes some inspiration from Silverstone and Hockenheim.

It's a mix of fast corners, long straights and has one of the steepest elevation climbs to Turn 1.

Most poles: Hamilton (2007, 2016-2018) is tied with Michael Schumacher (2000-2002, 2006) on four. Other pole sitters from the current grid are Verstappen (2021 and 2025), Carlos Sainz (2022), Leclerc (2023) and Lando Norris (2024).

Weather forecast

The weather for the United States Grand Prix is expected to be light rain with a gentle breeze throughout the course of the weekend, with highs of 32°C.

What happened last time out?
Verstappen edged out Norris to take an imperious pole position by 0.291 seconds.

The Red Bull driver dominated the race and posed as a serious threat to McLaren's Norris and Oscar Piastri in the drivers' championship.

Norris finished second and cut his lead to 14 points to Piastri in the standings, who finished fifth. Verstappen ended the weekend only 40 points behind Piastri with five races left of the season.

Who will win this year?

Antonelli will be as focused as ever to claim his ninth victory of the season with one hand already on the drivers' championship trophy.

However, Mercedes are still working on how to best optimise its current upgrade package. Last time out in Singapore, the team ran Russell on the older specification, while Antonelli had the upgraded package.

Red Bull were labelled by rivals as the "team to beat" for the remaining six races of the season. There seems to be no stopping Verstappen, who has won the U.S. Grand Prix four times.

Don't count out Hamilton who holds the record for six wins around COTA and will be looking to get his seventh podium for Ferrari this season.

stories.headline: St. Louis GK Bürki stretchered off after collision in Open Cup final
stories.summary: St. Louis goalkeeper Roman Bürki was taken to the hospital after taking a knock to the head during the U.S. Open Cup final against the Columbus Crew.
stories.body:
St. Louis City goalkeeper Roman Bürki was taken to the hospital after taking a knock to the head in a collision during his team's U.S. Open Cup final win over the Columbus Crew on Wednesday night.

In an attempt to make a save in the 70th minute, Bürki took a knee to the head from Crew winger Anass Zaroury. He remained on the ground to receive medical attention before being stretchered off the field.

Bürki was able to wave to supporters as he was taken away from the pitch. St. Louis confirmed to ESPN that Bürki was conscious and moving all extremities on his way to the hospital.

The score was tied 0-0 at the time of the injury, but St. Louis went on to win the game in a shootout after Burki's backup Ben Lundt made a save to help his team beat the Crew 5-3 on spot kicks.

The win earned St. Louis, which began play in MLS in 2023, its first trophy in club history.

St. Louis City captain Bürki had 43 touches and three crucial saves before the injury. He played an integral role in maintaining the 0-0 draw before being replaced by Lundt after the head injury.

Bürki, who joined St. Louis from Borussia Dortmund in 2022, stopped a corner kick from Brais Méndez that appeared to be goalbound and a flurry of other shots just before sustaining his injury.

Eleven minutes of injury time was added due to Bürki's injury, but neither team scored before the end of regulation despite Columbus outshooting St. Louis 16-3, so the game went to extra time and penalties.

stories.headline: Way-too-early AFL tiers: There's a clear flag favourite; 'silly season' winners and losers
stories.summary: Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL season is done and dusted, but that hasn't stopped ESPN's senior writer Jake Michaels from turning his attention to next year. Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers!

All of our best footy content, now on Instagram. Follow @espnfooty here!

Your new premiership favourite

1. HAWTHORN

Who knows if the Hawks would have been premiers this year if not for Hugh McCluggage's heroics late in that dramatic preliminary final at the MCG. There's certainly a real argument they would have gone all the way. This side, which is expertly coached by Sam Mitchell, just added Zach Merrett and Ben King to its best 23, two more experienced players desperate for flag success. There won't be many games the Hawks don't start favourite in next year. Even if this club's 2027 season over/under was set at preliminary final weekend, I'd still be taking the over.

Should be great, but there are some questions

2. BRISBANE

3. FREMANTLE

4. SYDNEY

The Lions just completed a remarkable three-peat and it certainly wouldn't have been outrageous for them to hold top spot here. But losing Lachie Neale and Chris Fagan -- arguably the two most important pieces of the club's modern-day dynasty -- cannot be underestimated. How do they fill those seismic gaps? The Dockers were the dominant team of the home and away season and if we played out the last four minutes of the Grand Final 100 times they probably win 99 of them. Instead, Fremantle has to spend all offseason dwelling on the greatest missed opportunity in club history. How do they respond in 2027? As for the Swans, who are always somewhere around the mark, nobody can really be sure what to expect after the Pullman Hotel saga. So many fascinating questions.

Silly season winners

5. GEELONG

6. WESTERN BULLDOGS

7. CARLTON

8. COLLINGWOOD

Each of these teams will be counting down the days until the 2027 season after drastically improving their lists during the trade and free agency window. The Cats landed the dynamic Toby Greene, significantly upgraded their ruck department with the singing of Rowan Marshall, and bolstered their defensive stocks with Jordan Ridley. The Bulldogs scored the biggest prize of all in Zak Butters, but they were also able to pry away Jordon Butts from the Crows, a much needed acquisition to what's been a shaky defence. The Blues will go into next season with Joel Amartey, Lachie Whitfield, and almost certainly father-son talent Cody Walker, while the Magpies added dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale and 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan.

Silly season losers

9. MELBOURNE

10. ADELAIDE

While a bunch of teams we'd expect to be in the fifth-to-10th range clearly improved their best 23, the Demons and Crows did nothing of the sort. Adelaide literally brought in nobody and will have to deal with the loss of key defender Jordon Butts, who departed as a free agent for the Bulldogs. Melbourne did sign several names, but do we think any of Zane Duursma, Will McLachlan, and Bodie Ryan can be needle movers in 2027? But hey, these were two sides I was down on this year and both ultimately outperformed expectations. Perhaps they do have it all figured out...

It's now or never

11. GOLD COAST

12. NORTH MELBOURNE

13. ST KILDA

If not now, then when? The Suns rocketed to co-flag favouritism this time last year after signing Christian Petracca and Jamarra Ugle-Hagan. They ultimately won just nine games and finished 13th on the ladder. Disastrous. Damien Hardwick is under serious pressure to get more out of this list. Meanwhile, the Kangaroos haven't played finals in a decade, but there's some newfound optimism after the senior coaching appointment of highly regarded Jaymie Graham and the signing of Nick Blakey, the biggest name the club has attracted in a decade. The Saints also need to show something early in 2027 or Ross Lyon could be on his way out ... again! But the real worry is not doing enough to ensure star midfielder Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera signs on.

It's going to be another long year

14. PORT ADELAIDE

15. GWS

16. WEST COAST

17. RICHMOND

18. ESSENDON

Perhaps I'm being a tad harsh on Port, who were pretty competitive this year. But at the end of the day we're taking Zak Butters out of a side that won just seven games. The Giants lost four of their best players in Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield, and Kieren Briggs, and will be relying heavily on their younger talent next year. And then there's the Eagles, Tigers, and Bombers -- three teams that combined for just nine wins this year. We all expect these sides to be somewhere around the bottom of the ladder.
